approved: Education Services for Overseas Students (Registration Charges) Amendment Bill 2021
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would raise fees for international education providers registered on CRICOS to recover the government's regulatory costs.
It would update the Registration Charges Act so that the Tertiary Education Quality Standards Agency, the Australian Skills Quality Authority and a department secretary can set their own charges.
The annual charges and application fees would be set by regulation, which could also exempt whole classes of providers.
The bill updates registration charges under the Registration Charges Act.
It lets ESOS agencies set their own cost recovery arrangements.
It allows regulations to prescribe charge amounts and indexation.
It allows regulations to exempt classes of providers from charges.

The majority voted in favour of *disagreeing* with an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2021-08-09.28.8) introduced by Moreton MP [Graham Perrett](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/moreton/graham_perrett) (Labor), which means it failed. The amendment would have added the words below to the usual [second reading motion](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/), which is *that the bill be read a second time* (parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill). ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House notes:* > > *(1) that the Government has damaged Australia's world-class higher education system, placing thousands of university workers' jobs at risk, and jeopardising Australian research; and* > > *(2) the Government's actions will make it harder for Australia to recover from the COVID-19 recession".*

The bill amends the Education Services for Overseas Students (Registration Charges) Act 1997 to implement an updated cost-recovery model for CRICOS registration charges, reducing provider payments by approximately $7 million per year. From 1 January 2022, only the Department of Education, Skills and Employment's regulatory costs will be recovered under this Act, with ASQA and TEQSA charging separately under their own frameworks.

The bill amends the Education Services for Overseas Students (TPS Levies) Act 2012 to add a definition of "total enrolments" for calculating Tuition Protection Service levies, clarifying that an enrolment counts when a student has enrolled and undertaken study in the relevant period. The new charging arrangements will commence from 1 January 2022.

The speaker supported the bills as they reduce charges on international education providers by $7 million a year, but criticised the Morrison government for damaging higher education, jeopardising jobs and research, and using ministerial discretion to avoid parliamentary scrutiny.

The Morrison government was accused of deliberately excluding universities from JobKeeper, costing at least 17,300 university jobs in 2020 and risking 7,000 researcher jobs, while neglecting a $40 billion export industry built on overseas students.

The speaker supported the Education Services for Overseas Students (Registration Charges) Amendment Bill 2021 and related bills, noting the Gold Coast international education sector contributed $1.6 billion to the local economy and $40 billion nationally before COVID-19, and highlighted $30 billion in federal support, $53 million in targeted aid, and $17.7 million in regulatory fee relief. Three Moncrieff electorates—Inforum Education Australia, Shafston International College, and BROWNS English Language School—each received $149,500 in innovation grants.

The Labor member supported the Education Services for Overseas Students bills to streamline cost recovery for international education providers, arguing the bills would reduce charges and prevent double charging. The member criticised the government for undermining the university sector, citing 18,000-30,000 job losses, fee increases of up to 113% for some degrees, and a projected 10% real funding cut over three years.

The Education Services for Overseas Students (Registration Charges) Amendment Bill 2021 was supported, shifting cost-recovery for CRICOS registration to individual ESOS agencies (ASQA, TEQSA, and the department). Labor supported the bill to streamline cost recovery and reduce charges for international education providers, but argued the Morrison government has abandoned universities by excluding them from JobKeeper, causing over 18,000 job losses and 30,000 fewer higher education workers. The speech also cited fee hikes of 113% for arts degrees and 28% for law and commerce, a drop in international education revenue from $40 billion to $22 billion, and the threat to La Trobe University's history department.

The speaker argued that the government's higher education legislation does not fix fee issues but instead increases fees by up to 113 percent for some degrees, imposes a $60,000 debt on students, and cuts university funding by 10 percent, while 17,000 staff have lost jobs and universities were denied JobKeeper.

The speaker argued that the government has failed to support Australia's international education sector during the pandemic, citing $37.5 billion in annual export earnings, 130,000 university jobs, 17,300 job losses, $3.8 billion in revenue loss for 2021, and 7,000 lost research positions. He called for dedicated quarantine facilities like Bladin Point in Darwin to safely bring back international students, criticising hotel quarantine leaks and the government's lack of a plan.

Labor supported the Education Services for Overseas Students (Registration Charges) Amendment Bill 2021 and cognate bills, which streamline cost-recovery for regulating international student education providers, but raised concerns that key details would be set by regulation rather than legislation, undermining transparency and accountability. The member for Sydney, member for Moreton, and member for Curtin were commended for their contributions.

The speaker argued that the Education Services for Overseas Students (Registration Charges) Amendment Bill 2021 is irrelevant because the Morrison government’s failures in quarantine and JobKeeper exclusion have decimated overseas student numbers, citing 21,000 university job losses nationally and 300 at Deakin University. The speaker also criticised the government’s higher education funding cuts and fee increases for arts and humanities students.

The speaker argued that the bill imposes a cost recovery model on international education at the worst possible time, noting the sector lost $40 billion in value pre-COVID and faces billions more in losses, with 18,000–21,000 university jobs cut. They criticised the government for refusing JobKeeper to universities, the Prime Minister for telling students to 'go home', and called for extending 485 visas, more business aid, and a recovery strategy from the Education Minister.

The Morrison government was criticised for failing to support universities during the pandemic by excluding them from JobKeeper and not building purpose-built quarantine facilities, resulting in job losses such as 277 at Monash University. The speech also called for greater investment in higher education and acknowledged the sacrifices made by young Australians.

The speaker announced a package of four bills introducing updated cost recovery arrangements for the Commonwealth Register of Institutions and Courses for Overseas Students (CRICOS) from 1 January 2022, which will reduce departmental charges. The amendments align with the Australian Government Charging Framework and aim to maintain quality and support recovery in the international education sector.
